Overview: Polyploidy in apple and what “triploid parent genetic material viability” means
- In cultivated apple (Malus × domestica), ploidy varies: most commercial varieties are diploid, but numerous triploid and tetraploid forms occur in collections and breeding lines, with tetraploids often used as intermediates to generate triploids via chromosome doubling or direct crosses.<cite id="30d267ea-0">While most apple varieties are diploid, ploidy levels vary across the species, and triploids may be used in breeding despite poor fertility.</cite> <cite id="30d267ea-2">In the Defra National Fruit Collection of 2,165 accessions, 304 (14%) were triploid; tetraploids are rarer but are often artificially created and used to develop triploid genotypes.</cite> <cite id="30d267ea-4">Wild apple M. hupehensis is triploid and allopolyploid, illustrating polyploidy in the genus and its genomic challenges.</cite>
- “Triploid parent genetic material viability” concerns whether genetic material contributed by a triploid parent can enter and establish in offspring, and whether resulting progeny are viable. In sexual reproduction, nuclear DNA from a triploid parent can enter seeds either as the embryo (if the triploid contributes a gamete) or as part of the hybrid endosperm (if the triploid contributes parental genomes to a cross). Cytoplasmic genetic material is typically maternally inherited. The viability of these products depends on meiotic regularity, gamete compatibility, and the endosperm’s genomic balance, which can be disrupted by triploidy (the “triploid block”).<cite id="9be1cfe0-3">One of the critical mechanisms contributing to reproductive isolation is the ‘triploid block’, where hybrid seeds formed between parents of different ploidy levels fail to develop properly due to disruption of the 2:1 maternal-to-paternal genomic ratio in the endosperm, leading to abnormal endosperm development and embryo arrest.</cite>

Polyploidy in apple: frequencies, traits, and breeding context
- Collections and cultivars: <cite id="30d267ea-2">About 14% of apple accessions in a national collection were triploid, and many economically important cultivars (e.g., Gravenstein, Baldwin, Stayman Winesap, Tompkins King, Jonagold, Mutsu) are triploid.</cite> <cite id="4b59899d-0">Triploid apples often have large fruits and have been widely adopted by growers and consumers; however, their fertility is generally lower than in diploids and tetraploids, with cultivar-specific differences, and breeders have historically struggled to release triploid cultivars via chromosome doubling or endosperm culture; most successful triploids have arisen from diploid crosses (sexual polyploidization).</cite>
- Traits and selection: <cite id="30d267ea-0">A SNP-based study of 970 accessions found triploids had significantly higher phenolic content after multiple-testing correction, but overall phenotypic differences across 10 traits were subtle and often insignificant, complicating the case for broad trait benefits from ploidy change.</cite>
- Crosses producing triploids: <cite id="30d267ea-3">Cytological screening of 2x × 4x crosses yielded mostly triploid hybrids; for example, 99% triploid (2n=51) in one family, 100% in others, with some diploid segregants; when the 4x was maternal, triploid frequencies ranged from 79–94%, depending on parent combination.</cite> These data show that controlled crosses can efficiently generate triploid apple seedlings, although their fertility and agronomic value are variable.<cite id="30d267ea-1">Uneven ploidy causes fewer balanced gametes and reduced fertility, making triploids challenging breeding parents, and historically they have been dubbed “breeding dead ends” due to rare offspring production despite claimed benefits.</cite>

Can a triploid parent contribute viable genetic material to offspring? Mechanisms and outcomes
- General plant mechanisms limiting triploid-to-offspring transmission via seed
  - Endosperm genomic balance: <cite id="9be1cfe0-3">The endosperm requires a 2:1 maternal-to-paternal genomic ratio for normal development; deviations caused by differing ploidy of parents disrupt endosperm cellularization and lead to embryo arrest, a mechanism central to the triploid block.</cite> <cite id="9be1cfe0-0">Triploid seeds are frequently aborted mainly due to endosperm–embryo unbalance; interploidy crosses often show low fruit-set percentages, reflecting strong postzygotic barriers when a triploid is involved.</cite>
  - Parental-ploidy asymmetry: <cite id="9be1cfe0-3">Maternal-excess crosses (4x × 2x) typically produce precocious endosperm cellularization and mostly viable seeds, whereas paternal-excess (2x × 4x) often cause delayed cellularization and seed collapse; this asymmetry explains why triploid-derived gametes as maternal (2n egg from a 3x) can fare better than paternal contributions.</cite>
  - Unreduced gametes and polyspermy: <cite id="9be1cfe0-0">Triploid parents can produce unreduced gametes; in red clover, tetraploid embryos from 4x–2x crosses survived while triploid-derived embryos were not, illustrating strong triploid blocks in that species, although outcomes can vary by system.</cite> <cite id="9be1cfe0-4">Selective egg-cell polyspermy can bypass the triploid block by adding multiple paternal copies to the embryo while the endosperm remains functional, enabling polyploid embryo development despite the usual triploid endosperm abortion; this pathway combines multiple genomes in one seed and represents a natural route to polyploidy relevant to inheritance.</cite>
- Evidence from apple and rosaceous crops
  - Predictable triploid progeny from 2x × 4x crosses: <cite id="30d267ea-3">Large-scale cytology of 2x × 4x crosses produced 79–99% triploid seedlings depending on parent pair, demonstrating that triploid nuclear DNA can be transmitted deterministically from defined parents in apple.</cite> <cite id="4b59899d-2">Crossing different-chromosomal apple forms (diploid × tetraploid or vice versa) generally yields triploid progeny; output of polyploid plants in progeny varies from 0 to 100% depending on pollinizer and parent quality, underscoring that seed transmission of triploid nuclear DNA is possible but variable.</cite>
  - Fertility and seed viability in triploid-derived progeny: <cite id="4b59899d-0">Triploid apple cultivars often have lower fertility than diploids and tetraploids, though not always zero and with cultivar-specific differences; thus, the viability of “genetic material” from a triploid parent can be high (as DNA that successfully fertilizes and forms seed), but the resulting plants may be less fertile as parents in subsequent generations.</cite> <cite id="9be1cfe0-1">In woody ornamentals, triploid hybrids are often bred to be sterile for unique traits, yet some triploid parents produce fertile offspring; for example, triploid Hydrangea macrophylla cultivars showed higher stainable pollen percentages than some diploids and produced fertile progeny, though aneuploid offspring were frequent, indicating that gamete viability does not guarantee euploid, perfectly fertile progeny.</cite>
  - Constraints in specific crosses: <cite id="9be1cfe0-2">In grass species, crosses between diploid female and tetraploid male can produce triploid embryos but suffer high embryo abortion (up to 92% nonviable seeds), with only 4.5% triploid plants observed in one case; this highlights that even when nuclear DNA from a triploid parent enters the zygote, endosperm or pairing incompatibilities can abort the seed or yield sterile triploids.</cite>

Why triploids are often “breeding dead ends” in apple and what that means for viability
- Meiotic irregularity reduces seed set: <cite id="30d267ea-1">Triploids have uneven ploidy leading to fewer balanced gametes and reduced fertility, which historically limited their ability to produce viable offspring and led to their designation as “breeding dead ends.”</cite> <cite id="30d267ea-3">Even when triploid seedlings are produced from 2x × 4x crosses, their fertility as parents is variable and often inferior, contributing to the perception that triploids stall breeding progress.</cite>
- Pollination and seed requirements in apple: <cite id="4b59899d-3">Apple flowers are self-sterile due to gametophytic self-incompatibility, and most cultivars require cross-pollen to set fruit; seedless cultivars arise by parthenocarpy, but normal fruit require at least one developing embryo per carpel to trigger hormone-driven shape formation.</cite> <cite id="4b59899d-4">Therefore, triploid parents’ reduced fertility directly impacts seed formation and fruit set; even if triploid cytoplasmic or nuclear material enters progeny, low seed viability and irregular meiosis reduce the chance of producing fertile, set-producing triploid parents.</cite>

Triploid parents and cytoplasmic vs nuclear genetic material in offspring
- Cytoplasmic inheritance and the maternal effect: In sexual seed production, the embryo’s cytoplasm is predominantly maternal; thus, a triploid parent acting as seed parent can pass along its maternal cytoplasm to triploid or euploid progeny, whereas a triploid acting as pollen parent contributes little cytoplasm to the zygote. Endosperm development depends on the maternal-to-paternal nuclear ratio; cytoplasmic incompatibilities are less directly implicated than genomic balance, but can compound failures in crosses with ploidy mismatch.<cite id="9be1cfe0-3">Disruptions in the 2:1 maternal-to-paternal genomic ratio in the endosperm are central to triploid seed failure; cytoplasmic contributions are secondary, but maternal cytoplasm largely determines the embryo’s organelles regardless of ploidy outcome.</cite>
- Practical implication for “viability of genetic material”: 
  - If a triploid is the seed parent (providing a 2n egg), triploid nuclear DNA will enter the zygote and be transmitted to the embryo; with appropriate parental combinations, many apple 2x × 4x crosses yield >75–95% triploid seedlings, indicating high viability of the nuclear genetic material delivered via seed, although these seedlings often have reduced fertility as parents themselves.<cite id="30d267ea-3">In multiple 2x × 4x families, 79–99% of seedlings were triploid, demonstrating high transmission of triploid nuclear DNA via seed when the maternal parent is tetraploid and the paternal is diploid.</cite> 
  - If a triploid is the pollen parent (1n sperm), the zygote receives triploid nuclear DNA only if the sperm is unreduced (2n); otherwise the embryo is diploid. Endosperm formed from 2x (mother) × 2n (triploid sperm) is tetraploid and may function, but from 2x × 1n triploid sperm the endosperm is 3x and typically fails (triploid block), aborting the seed.<cite id="9be1cfe0-3">When maternal-to-paternal nuclear ratio deviates from 2:1 in the endosperm, embryo arrest follows; thus, 2x × 1n triploid sperm leads to 3x endosperm and seed abortion, while rare 2x × 2n sperm (unreduced) yields viable triploid zygotes.</cite> <cite id="9be1cfe0-0">Unreduced gametes from triploids can occur; their union with haploid gametes can yield triploid zygotes, but triploid seeds are frequently aborted due to the endosperm–embryo imbalance (triploid block).</cite>
- Cytoplasmic gene flow is mostly maternal; triploid-derived cytoplasm can be fixed in the embryo if the triploid is the seed parent, but triploid fertility as a pollen parent limits paternal cytoplasmic transmission. Polyspermy-derived embryos can receive multiple paternal genomes while evading endosperm abortion, enabling cytoplasm-ambiguous but genome-combined polyploid embryos in rare cases.<cite id="9be1cfe0-4">Selective egg-cell polyspermy can add multiple paternal copies to the embryo while leaving the endosperm intact, bypassing the triploid block and producing polyploid embryos that combine multiple genomes; such seeds represent a one-step three-genome hybridization route.</cite>

How to increase viability when using triploid parents in apple
- Choose parental combinations to favor euploid embryo rescue: <cite id="9be1cfe0-3">Maternal-excess crosses (4x female × 2x male) often yield mostly viable seeds, whereas paternal-excess crosses (2x × 4x) frequently abort; thus, using a triploid as maternal parent (via a 4x female) increases the likelihood that triploid-derived maternal genomes integrate into viable embryos.</cite> <cite id="30d267ea-3">Empirically, multiple 2x × 4x families yielded triploid seedlings at very high frequency when the maternal line was 4x, with 79–94% triploid depending on cultivar combination, showing practical feasibility when maternal ploidy is optimized.</cite>
- Screen for unreduced gametes and fertility in triploid parents: <cite id="9be1cfe0-1">Triploid fertility is cultivar-specific; some triploid apple cultivars have higher pollen staining and produce fertile offspring, indicating that identifying fertile, unreduced-gamete-producing triploids can improve seed transmission.</cite> <cite id="9be1cfe0-0">Breeders often encounter absolute sterility in triploid hybrids; however, interspecific or ornamental species show variability, and screening for unreduced gametes can identify triploids that restore sexual seed production.</cite>
- Leverage vegetative/clonal propagation when sexual viability is low: <cite id="4b59899d-0">Because sexual fertility of triploids is generally lower than diploids and tetraploids, most successful triploid cultivars in apple are obtained via sexual polyploidization from diploid parents; yet, once triploids are obtained, vegetative propagation is the primary route to fix desirable triploid traits, and chromosome doubling attempts in the past have rarely yielded market-ready cultivars.</cite> This underscores that triploid “genetic material” can be conserved and widely multiplied as clones even if sexual seed transmission is unreliable.

Practical expectations for apple breeding and beyond
- What to expect from triploid parents:
  - High viability of nuclear DNA from a triploid seed parent into the embryo is common in 2x × 4x crosses, yielding triploid seedlings; however, these seedlings often have reduced fertility, so further sexual breeding is impeded.<cite id="30d267ea-3">Triploid frequencies up to 99% in 2x × 4x crosses show efficient nuclear DNA transmission via seed when maternal ploidy is favorable.</cite> <cite id="4b59899d-0">Triploid apple seedlings frequently show lower fertility than diploids/tetraploids, which has hindered their deployment as sexual parents.</cite>
  - Seed viability can be low when the triploid is a pollen parent or when genomic ratios are unbalanced; using triploids as seed parents (or via maternal tetraploids) and screening for unreduced gametes improves success, but crosses with diploid female parents often abort seeds or yield sterile triploids.<cite id="9be1cfe0-3">Abnormal endosperm development from 2:1 ratio disruption leads to embryo arrest, a major reason triploid hybrid seeds abort.</cite> <cite id="9be1cfe0-2">Diploid female × tetraploid male crosses can yield many nonviable seeds due to incompatibility or meiotic errors, with only a small fraction of triploid plants produced.</cite>
  - Cytoplasmic material from a triploid parent is mainly maternal; paternal triploid cytoplasm contributes only rarely due to low fertility of triploid pollen. Polyspermy can create rare exceptions where multiple paternal genomes reach the embryo while endosperm function is preserved, enabling polyploid embryo rescue and cytoplasm-ambiguous combinations.<cite id="9be1cfe0-4">Selective egg-cell polyspermy bypasses the triploid block by transmitting multiple paternal copies to the embryo, allowing polyploid embryo development and three-genome combinations.</cite>
- Apple-specific notes: <cite id="4b59899d-0">Famous triploid cultivars (Jonagold, Mutsu) arose from diploid crosses; tetraploids are deliberately used to rescue euploid gametes for seedling production, and breeders now use co-dominant markers to rapidly identify triploid seedlings among large populations to accelerate selection.</cite> <cite id="30d267ea-1">Triploid cultivars may show larger fruit and disease resistance but uneven fertility makes them difficult to breed forward; historical pedigrees suggest they played a role but were often rare producers of offspring, reinforcing their status as partial “dead ends.”</cite>
- Context from other rosaceous species: <cite id="9be1cfe0-0">In Medicago, tetraploid females accepted crosses and triploid seeds were frequent, but triploid block strength varied; in red clover, 4x–2x crosses produced tetraploid embryos while triploid ones aborted, illustrating species-specific triploid constraints.</cite> <cite id="9be1cfe0-1">In Hydrangea macrophylla, triploids show cultivar-specific fertility and can produce fertile offspring, countering the absolute sterility stereotype and showing that cytoplasmic-genome combinations can be viable under certain conditions.</cite>

Bottom line answers to the user’s question
- How common is polyploidy in apple? <cite id="30d267ea-2">Triploids constitute roughly 14% of accessions in one national collection, and many commercial cultivars are triploid; tetraploids are less common but used to generate triploids.</cite>
- Can a triploid parent pass on viable genetic material? 
  - Yes, if used as a seed (female) parent: <cite id="30d267ea-3">Crosses between diploid pollen and tetraploid seed parents yield mostly triploid seedlings (79–99%), indicating high viability of nuclear DNA from the triploid parent delivered to the embryo.</cite> <cite id="4b59899d-2">Different-chromosomal crosses (2x × 4x) commonly produce triploid progeny (0–100% depending on cultivar), confirming transfer of triploid nuclear DNA into viable seedlings.</cite>
  - Viability depends on genomic balance and gamete ploidy: <cite id="9be1cfe0-3">Triploid blocks from 2:1 endosperm ratio disruption commonly abort embryos, especially in paternal-excess crosses; maternal-excess crosses fare better, and cultivar-specific meiosis (unreduced gametes) can enable successful transmission.</cite> <cite id="9be1cfe0-4">Polyspermy can selectively add paternal genomes to the embryo while preserving endosperm function, bypassing the triploid block and yielding viable polyploid embryos in rare but reproducible cases.</cite>
  - Cytoplasmic material is mostly maternal; triploid pollen parents contribute cytoplasm rarely due to low fertility, while seed parents can pass along triploid-derived maternal cytoplasm.
- Why are triploids often “dead ends” in apple breeding? <cite id="30d267ea-1">Uneven ploidy yields fewer balanced gametes and reduced fertility, limiting seed set and offspring production; historically triploids rarely produced viable offspring, reinforcing their limited use as sexual parents despite desirable agronomic traits.</cite> <cite id="4b59899d-0">Even when triploid seedlings are produced, their lower fertility compared to diploids/tetraploids slows breeding progress; most successful triploid cultivars derive from diploid crosses rather than chromosome doubling.</cite>
- Alternatives when using triploid material: <cite id="4b59899d-0">Triploid cultivars are widely propagated vegetatively to fix traits, and modern marker-assisted protocols rapidly identify triploid seedlings for orchard use or clonal multiplication.</cite> <cite id="30d267ea-2">Tetraploids can be used as parents to rescue euploid gametes (2n eggs) for crossing with diploids to produce triploid hybrids at high frequency.</cite>
- What to expect in your system: 
  - If you use a triploid as the seed parent, expect high transmission of triploid nuclear DNA into the embryo, and screen progeny for fertility and trait value; expect frequent success when the maternal parent is tetraploid and the paternal diploid, with many triploid seedlings surviving to seed orchard stages.<cite id="30d267ea-3">High percentages (79–99%) of triploid seedlings from 2x × 4x crosses demonstrate this approach’s power.</cite>
  - If you use a triploid as the pollen parent, expect low seed set due to triploid block and meiotic irregularity; consider using triploid cultivars as clonal standards for pollination services rather than expecting fertile seed, and test for unreduced gamete producers to improve rates.<cite id="4b59899d-0">Triploid pollen fertility is often lower than diploid, limiting seed production; cultivar-by-cultivar exceptions exist.</cite>

A break of the self-incompatibility system, allowing self-fertilization in tetraploid female plants, cannot be completely ruled out, as self-incompatibility systems may be broken down by polyploidy (Otto & Whitton, 2000). However, as apparently no endogamic depression was observed in the derived plants, this possibility seems unlikely. 

Interploidy crosses tend to be more successful when the tetraploid is the female parent, as was the case in the parental generation of the present work, as the endosperm-embryo balance will be more similar to the normal rule (Bretagnolle & Thompson, 1995). It is ordinarily stated that triploid seeds are frequently aborted mainly due to endosperm-embryo unbalance (Ramsey & Schemske, 1998;Beuselinck et al., 2003), and this post-zigotic reproductive barrier is called triploid block. That could explain the low percentage of seed formed in the first cross (6.56% of the pollinated flowers produced seed) (Figure 1). 

Working with red clover, Parrott & Smith (1984) reported that tetraploid embryos resulting from 4x-2x crosses survived, but not the triploid ones, which led the authors to suggest that in this species the triploid block is very strong and, consequently, only tetraploid progeny is produced. However, our results lead to different conclusions.

Title: Transcriptomic insights into triploid seed failure in Arabidopsis arenosa natural populations
Snippet: Polyploidy, or whole-genome duplication (WGD), is a major driver of plant speciation and adaptation (Soltis & Soltis, 2012). It has been estimated that 15 % of speciation events in flowering plants were associated with change in ploidy (Wood et al., 2009) and when a higher extinction rates in neopolyploids are taken into account, polyploid speciation rates may be even higher up to 30% (Mayrose et al., 2011). Newly formed polyploids often become immediately reproductively isolated from their diploid progenitors, restricting gene flow and promoting genetic divergence (Ramsey & Schemske, 1998, Husband & Sabara, 2004). One of the critical mechanisms contributing to this reproductive isolation is the "triploid block", where hybrid seeds formed between parents of different ploidy levels fail to develop properly (Scott et al., 1998;Köhler et al., 2010;Lafon-Placette & Köhler, 2016). This seed inviability is typically caused by disruptions in the strict 2:1 maternal-to-paternal genomic ratio in the endosperm, which is essential for normal seed development (Haig & Westoby, 1989). 

Deviations from this ratio can lead to abnormal endosperm development, such as over-proliferation or impaired cellularization, both of which ultimately result in embryo arrest (Erilova et al., 2009;Lafon-Placette & Köhler, 2016). 

Much of the mechanistic understanding of the triploid block comes from studies in A. 

thaliana. In this model species, paternal-excess crosses (2x × 4x; the seed parent is always designated first) often cause delayed endosperm cellularization leading to seed collapse, whereas maternal-excess crosses (4x × 2x) typically result in precocious endosperm cellularization and mostly viable seeds (Scott et al., 1998).
</snippet>

Title: Selective egg cell polyspermy bypasses the triploid block
Snippet: The triploid block is an established and widely distributed postzygotic hybridization barrier. In light of its fatal consequence, it has been suggested that there are ways to overcome this hybridization barrier (Ko ¨hler et al., 2010). We here established a novel polyspermy detection assay that allows to identify and characterize developing embryos resulting from supernumerary sperm fusion. With this tool we were able to show that most polyspermy-derived plants develop from seeds resulting from selective egg cell polyploidization. In those seeds, supernumerary paternal copies are only transmitted to the embryo, thereby bypassing the triploid block of the endosperm. Our results expand previous polyploidization concepts, which state that the increase in genome copies is caused by infrequent meiotic or mitotic defects. In fact, the currently favored route towards polyploid plants involves unreduced male gametes; however, this scenario introduces supernumerary paternal copies also to the endosperm, which is not tolerated in many plants resulting in seed abortion (Dilkes et al., 2008;Ramsey and Schemske, 1998;Scott et al., 1998;Stoute et al., 2012). In fact, this endosperm-related triploid block is considered a means of reproductive isolation (Ko ¨hler et al., 2010;Ramsey and Schemske, 1998). Plant polyploidization via polyspermy, by contrast, often affects the embryo-derived seed fraction only and hence has the potential to bypass the triploid block. It will be a challenge for the future to determine whether and to what extent polyspermy is relevant in nature and contributed to the evolution of polyploid plants. 

From an evolutionary and agricultural point of view, another intriguing implication of polyspermyinduced polyploidization is the one-step combination of three genetically distinct plant genomes in a three-parent hybridization. This scenario is expected to occur rarely in nature, even when taking into account wind and animal pollination. Still, it might be relevant in an evolutionary time scale and when considering the huge seed amounts produced by many plants.

Snippet: Triploid apples, generally characterized by their large fruits, have been very attractive to both growers and consumers: old cultivars such as 'Gravenstein', 'Baldwin', 'Rhode Island Greening', 'Blenheim Orange', 'Stayman Winesap', 'Tompkins County King', as well as newer cultivars 'Jonagold' and 'Mutsu' [28]. The fertility of triploids has, however, been found to be lower than that of the diploids and tetraploids, but rarely zero and often with differences between cultivars [1], [9], [28]. This character appeals to both apple breeders and growers because of less labour needed for blossom and fruit thinning in triploids [28]. Despite years of effort, attempts of chromosome doubling using colchicine [36] and endosperm culture [28] have not contributed to release of triploid apple cultivars. More than 90% commercially superior triploid apple cultivars have proved to be produced by sexual polyploidization [28]. Thus, diploid crosses remain the principal method to breed apple triploid cultivars. 

There are approximately 8,000 diploid apple cultivars in the world, but fewer than 50 are triploids [28]. Given importance of triploid cultivars in the apple industry, we present a protocol using co-dominant markers aimed to efficiently identify a small number of triploid seedlings in a large population and thus to accelerate the triploid breeding program (Figure S1). In addition, parental genetic backgrounds influenced the frequency of triploids in the diploid F 1 seedlings (Table 1), thus parents should be carefully chosen for successful triploid breeding.

Title: Comparing diploid and triploid apples from a diverse collection
Snippet: Apples (Malus X. domestica Borkh.) are an economically important fruit species and the focus of continuing breeding efforts around the world. While most apple varieties are diploid, ploidy levels vary across the species, and triploids may be used in breeding despite poor fertility. The impact of ploidy on agricultural traits in apple is not well understood but is an important factor to consider when breeding new apple varieties. Here, we use mean heterozygosity values to categorize 970 apple accessions as diploid or triploid and then contrast apples of varying ploidy levels across 10 agriculturally important traits with sample sizes ranging from 427 to 928 accessions. After correction for multiple testing, we determine that triploids have significantly higher phenolic content. By examining historical release dates for apple varieties, our findings suggest that contemporary breeding programs are primarily releasing diploid varieties, and triploids tend to be older varieties. Ultimately, our results suggest that phenotypic differences between diploids and triploids are subtle and often insignificant indicating that triploids may not provide substantial benefit above diploids to apple breeding programs.
</snippet>

Generally, from crossings of different-chromosomal apple forms (diploid x tetraploid; tetraploid x diploid) the triploid progeny is formed. Title: Wind Pollination of Apple Flowers Under Insect Exclusion Nets Questions the Insect-Dependent Pollination Model of Modern Apple Plantations
Snippet: Flowers of domesticated apple (Malus × domestica Borkh.) are perfect and complete. Apple is regarded as a self-infertile member of the Rosaceae family whose outcrossing is facilitated by the gametophytic self-incompatibility (GSI) system requiring pollen donors to possess at least one different S allele than the pistil to facilitate fertilization [1]. Pollination is a necessary step in apple fruit development, except for seedless cultivars (e.g., Spencer Seedless', Wellington Bloomless', and Rae Ime') whose fruit originate parthenocarpically [2]. In rare cases, self-compatible and cross-incompatible cultivars exist, albeit they are few [3]; the latter is limited to genetically similar varieties such as Cortland, Macoun, and McIntosh, and sports of a cultivar [4]. Self-pollination studies have demonstrated varying levels of self-fertility, ranging from ~2% in 'Fuji' and 'Golden Delicious' to 8% and 12% for 'Elstar' and 'Idared', respectively [5]. 

Pollination of most tree fruit species, including apple, is considered insect-dependent (Entomophilous), purportedly due to the relative mass of tree fruit pollen [6], in contrast Plants 2025, 14, 1196 2 of 14 with anemophilous species such as nut trees that depend on wind for pollen dispersal. The primary apple pollinators comprise species of bees and hoverflies [4,7]; the former are highly effective pollinators of apple flowers [8] and, thus, are typically introduced to apple plantations as managed hives of European honeybees (Apis mellifera) to ensure adequate fruit set for commercial yield [4]. An important agronomic consequence of current apple pollination practices is the 'oversetting' of fruit, necessitating the additional expense and often unpredictable practice of chemical fruitlet thinning [9].
</snippet>

Title: Identification of pollinizers for apple ‘SCS426 Venice
Snippet: Although presenting hermaphrodite flowers, apples (Malus × domestica Borkh.) depend on cross-pollination for the fertilization of the flowers and consequent fruit set. This necessity is due to the gametophytic self-incompatibility mechanism presented in most species of the genus Malus and in several genera of the Rosaceae family (Fujii et al. 2016). Most apple cultivars do not produce fruit by self-pollination or by crosses between genotypes that have the same alleles in the S-locus, responsible for gametophytic self-incompatibility control (Ramírez and Davenport 2013;Kasajima 2017). 

For this reason, most commercial apple orchards are composed of fruit-producing cultivars (scion cultivars) and at least another genotype used as a pollinizer. Pollinizers must coincide at flowering time with the scion cultivar (Matsumoto 2014;Albuquerque Junior et al. 2011). In addition, scion cultivars and pollinizers need to be genetically compatible (Orcheski and Brown 2012), since the pollen tube does not grow when the S-allele in the haploid cell of the pollen grain is the same to one of the two S-alleles expressed in the pistil (Matsumoto et al. 1999;Sassa et al. 2007). 

The gametophytic self-incompatibility is a barrier to identify and use compatible plants for directed crosses or pollination in the field that enables fruit set (de Nettancourt 1977). Likewise, fruit growers cannot produce fruit optimally when incompatible genotypes are grown in the orchards (Orcheski and Brown 2012). In order to ensure the formation of symmetrical fruit with normal shape development, at least one seed must be formed in four of the five fruit carpels (Denardi and Stuker 2008;Sheffield 2014). The normal apple shape formation is induced through hormones released by the developing embryos, so the ovule fertilization and the consequent seed formation in the carpels are necessary to obtain fruit with appropriate shape (Matsumoto et al. 2012).

Overview: Polyploidy in apple and what “triploid parent genetic material viability” means
- In cultivated apple (Malus × domestica), ploidy varies: most commercial varieties are diploid, but numerous triploid and tetraploid forms occur in collections and breeding lines, with tetraploids often used as intermediates to generate triploids via chromosome doubling or direct crosses.<cite id="30d267ea-0">While most apple varieties are diploid, ploidy levels vary across the species, and triploids may be used in breeding despite poor fertility.</cite> <cite id="30d267ea-2">In the Defra National Fruit Collection of 2,165 accessions, 304 (14%) were triploid; tetraploids are rarer but are often artificially created and used to develop triploid genotypes.</cite> <cite id="30d267ea-4">Wild apple M. hupehensis is triploid and allopolyploid, illustrating polyploidy in the genus and its genomic challenges.</cite>
- “Triploid parent genetic material viability” concerns whether genetic material contributed by a triploid parent can enter and establish in offspring, and whether resulting progeny are viable. In sexual reproduction, nuclear DNA from a triploid parent can enter seeds either as the embryo (if the triploid contributes a gamete) or as part of the hybrid endosperm (if the triploid contributes parental genomes to a cross). Cytoplasmic genetic material is typically maternally inherited. The viability of these products depends on meiotic regularity, gamete compatibility, and the endosperm’s genomic balance, which can be disrupted by triploidy (the “triploid block”).<cite id="9be1cfe0-3">One of the critical mechanisms contributing to reproductive isolation is the ‘triploid block’, where hybrid seeds formed between parents of different ploidy levels fail to develop properly due to disruption of the 2:1 maternal-to-paternal genomic ratio in the endosperm, leading to abnormal endosperm development and embryo arrest.</cite>

- Collections and cultivars: <cite id="30d267ea-2">About 14% of apple accessions in a national collection were triploid, and many economically important cultivars (e.g., Gravenstein, Baldwin, Stayman Winesap, Tompkins King, Jonagold, Mutsu) are triploid.</cite> <cite id="4b59899d-0">Triploid apples often have large fruits and have been widely adopted by growers and consumers; however, their fertility is generally lower than in diploids and tetraploids, with cultivar-specific differences, and breeders have historically struggled to release triploid cultivars via chromosome doubling or endosperm culture; most successful triploids have arisen from diploid crosses (sexual polyploidization).</cite>
- Traits and selection: <cite id="30d267ea-0">A SNP-based study of 970 accessions found triploids had significantly higher phenolic content after multiple-testing correction, but overall phenotypic differences across 10 traits were subtle and often insignificant, complicating the case for broad trait benefits from ploidy change.</cite>
- Crosses producing triploids: <cite id="30d267ea-3">Cytological screening of 2x × 4x crosses yielded mostly triploid hybrids; for example, 99% triploid (2n=51) in one family, 100% in others, with some diploid segregants; when the 4x was maternal, triploid frequencies ranged from 79–94%, depending on parent combination.</cite> These data show that controlled crosses can efficiently generate triploid apple seedlings, although their fertility and agronomic value are variable.<cite id="30d267ea-1">Uneven ploidy causes fewer balanced gametes and reduced fertility, making triploids challenging breeding parents, and historically they have been dubbed “breeding dead ends” due to rare offspring production despite claimed benefits.</cite>

- General plant mechanisms limiting triploid-to-offspring transmission via seed
  - Endosperm genomic balance: <cite id="9be1cfe0-3">The endosperm requires a 2:1 maternal-to-paternal genomic ratio for normal development; deviations caused by differing ploidy of parents disrupt endosperm cellularization and lead to embryo arrest, a mechanism central to the triploid block.</cite> <cite id="9be1cfe0-0">Triploid seeds are frequently aborted mainly due to endosperm–embryo unbalance; interploidy crosses often show low fruit-set percentages, reflecting strong postzygotic barriers when a triploid is involved.</cite>

While most apple varieties are diploid, ploidy levels vary across the species, and triploids may be used in breeding despite poor fertility. Title: Sexual polyploidization in red clover
Snippet: The tetraploid plants found in the F 1 generation (Table 1) were most probably formed by the union of unreduced pollen grains of the Quiñiqueli plants and the oospheres of the tetraploid female plants, while tetraploids in the following generations could be formed by three ways: union of normal gametes of the former generation tetraploid plants, or by the union of a tetraploid plant normal gamete and a 2n gamete of a triploid plant, or by the union of two, 2n gametes of triploid plants. A break of the self-incompatibility system, allowing self-fertilization in tetraploid female plants, cannot be completely ruled out, as self-incompatibility systems may be broken down by polyploidy (Otto & Whitton, 2000). However, as apparently no endogamic depression was observed in the derived plants, this possibility seems unlikely. 

Interploidy crosses tend to be more successful when the tetraploid is the female parent, as was the case in the parental generation of the present work, as the endosperm-embryo balance will be more similar to the normal rule (Bretagnolle & Thompson, 1995). It is ordinarily stated that triploid seeds are frequently aborted mainly due to endosperm-embryo unbalance (Ramsey & Schemske, 1998;Beuselinck et al., 2003), and this post-zigotic reproductive barrier is called triploid block. That could explain the low percentage of seed formed in the first cross (6.56% of the pollinated flowers produced seed) (Figure 1). 

Working with red clover, Parrott & Smith (1984) reported that tetraploid embryos resulting from 4x-2x crosses survived, but not the triploid ones, which led the authors to suggest that in this species the triploid block is very strong and, consequently, only tetraploid progeny is produced. However, our results lead to different conclusions.

Title: Ploidy Level Influences Pollen Tube Growth and Seed Viability in Interploidy Crosses of Hydrangea macrophylla
Snippet: However, as proportion of unreduced gametes (determined by pollen visualization and experiments) is genotype-specific (Herben et al., 2016;Alexander, 2017) more triploid cultivars should be screened for unreduced gamete production. Sexual hybridization among ploidy levels has played a key role in breeding improvement for a large number of woody ornamental species where crosses between tetraploid and diploid parents are used to produce sterile triploid hybrids with unique traits (Kumari and George, 2008). Breeders often face strong or absolute sterility of triploid hybrids which prevents further breeding using triploid individuals. In the case of H. macrophylla, triploids have nearly identical fertility to diploids and that fertility is cultivar specific (Jones et al., 2007;Alexander, 2017). All three triploid cultivars used as parents in this study had a higher fertility (as measured by percent stainable pollen) than the least fertile diploid parent. Fertility of triploids determined by staining is corroborated by the presence of offspring in this and other studies, and by the results of pollen tube growth presented herein. The offspring were also fertile such that progeny with unique traits could be used for future breeding. However, the high number of aneuploid progeny indicates that aneuploid gametes appear viable using the staining method described herein.

Title: May the crossing between diploid and tetraploid Italian ryegrass transfer glyphosate resistance to the next generation?
Snippet: Thus, theoretically, the progeny from DRR♀ × TSC♂ crosses should have a triploid embryo and a tetraploid endosperm, whereas the seed coat should be diploid. However, high seed number without embryo (92% value) was found by the seed viability test (Table 1, Fig. 1). 

The incompatibility of chromosomal sets to form the embryo in DRR♀ × TSC♂ crosses can contribute strongly to the high percentage of nonviable seeds (Ruchel et al. 2015). Another possibility involves errors during the meiosis in diploid plants, in which the chromosomes fail to properly segregate to daughter cells. Thus, the unreduced gamete can unite with a haploid gamete, resulting in a triploid zygote that can originate a triploid plant. Sterile triploid plants were found to the crosses of diploid and tetraploid Centaurea seridis L. plants, which had chromosomes failure to pair correctly during the meiosis and provided a reproductive barrier (Ferriol et al. 2015). However, our results demonstrate only 4.5% of triploid plants to the crosses of DRR♀ with TSC♂.

Title: Transcriptomic insights into triploid seed failure in Arabidopsis arenosa natural populations
Snippet: Polyploidy, or whole-genome duplication (WGD), is a major driver of plant speciation and adaptation (Soltis & Soltis, 2012). It has been estimated that 15 % of speciation events in flowering plants were associated with change in ploidy (Wood et al., 2009) and when a higher extinction rates in neopolyploids are taken into account, polyploid speciation rates may be even higher up to 30% (Mayrose et al., 2011). Newly formed polyploids often become immediately reproductively isolated from their diploid progenitors, restricting gene flow and promoting genetic divergence (Ramsey & Schemske, 1998, Husband & Sabara, 2004). Title: Molecular Genetic Features of Polyploidization and Aneuploidization Reveal Unique Patterns for Genome Duplication in Diploid Malus
Snippet: Triploid apples, generally characterized by their large fruits, have been very attractive to both growers and consumers: old cultivars such as 'Gravenstein', 'Baldwin', 'Rhode Island Greening', 'Blenheim Orange', 'Stayman Winesap', 'Tompkins County King', as well as newer cultivars 'Jonagold' and 'Mutsu' [28]. The fertility of triploids has, however, been found to be lower than that of the diploids and tetraploids, but rarely zero and often with differences between cultivars [1], [9], [28]. This character appeals to both apple breeders and growers because of less labour needed for blossom and fruit thinning in triploids [28]. Despite years of effort, attempts of chromosome doubling using colchicine [36] and endosperm culture [28] have not contributed to release of triploid apple cultivars. More than 90% commercially superior triploid apple cultivars have proved to be produced by sexual polyploidization [28]. Thus, diploid crosses remain the principal method to breed apple triploid cultivars. 

There are approximately 8,000 diploid apple cultivars in the world, but fewer than 50 are triploids [28]. Given importance of triploid cultivars in the apple industry, we present a protocol using co-dominant markers aimed to efficiently identify a small number of triploid seedlings in a large population and thus to accelerate the triploid breeding program (Figure S1). In addition, parental genetic backgrounds influenced the frequency of triploids in the diploid F 1 seedlings (Table 1), thus parents should be carefully chosen for successful triploid breeding.

Title: Comparing diploid and triploid apples from a diverse collection
Snippet: Apples (Malus X. domestica Borkh.) are an economically important fruit species and the focus of continuing breeding efforts around the world. While most apple varieties are diploid, ploidy levels vary across the species, and triploids may be used in breeding despite poor fertility. The impact of ploidy on agricultural traits in apple is not well understood but is an important factor to consider when breeding new apple varieties. Here, we use mean heterozygosity values to categorize 970 apple accessions as diploid or triploid and then contrast apples of varying ploidy levels across 10 agriculturally important traits with sample sizes ranging from 427 to 928 accessions. After correction for multiple testing, we determine that triploids have significantly higher phenolic content. By examining historical release dates for apple varieties, our findings suggest that contemporary breeding programs are primarily releasing diploid varieties, and triploids tend to be older varieties. Ultimately, our results suggest that phenotypic differences between diploids and triploids are subtle and often insignificant indicating that triploids may not provide substantial benefit above diploids to apple breeding programs.

Title: Estimation of New Tetraploid Apple Forms as Donors of Diploid Gametes for Selection on a Polyploidy Level
Snippet: The tendency of the environmental deterioration through numerous stresses of the biological and technogenic character leads to the lowing of apple adaptativity and quality of apple production. So, breeders constantly have to improve the fruit assortment, replenish it with new cultivars with high resistance and adaptivity. Using polyploidy in apple breeding is one of the methods favoring the fulfilling of this goal. 

Generally, from crossings of different-chromosomal apple forms (diploid x tetraploid; tetraploid x diploid) the triploid progeny is formed. A high value of triploid apple cultivars was often confirmed (Tuz, Lozitsky, 1970 [1]; Bacharach ,1982 [2]; Singh, Wafai, 1984 [3]; Barletta, 1988 [4], etc.). It was noted that triploid cultivars not infrequently have higher economically valuable traits than diploid ones. In this connection, the mass obtaining of triploid hybrids will give a chance to select promising cultivars meeting the requirements of the intensive adaptive horticulture. A scanty set of initial tetraploid forms-donors of diploid gametes is one of the limited factors for a successful fulfillment of this goal. 

At the All Russian Research Institute of Fruit Crop Breeding the apple breeding on a polyploidy level has been carried out since 1970. For this period a number of triploid cultivars have been developed from different-chromosomal crossings. Part of them has been regionalized another part is on the state trials. Besides, a number of tetraploid forms have been obtained, which are of interest for use in further breeding. In breeding respect these forms are of equal value. In the hybrid progeny obtained from crossings of diploid cultivars with tetraploid forms when a tetraploid form is a pollinator, different pollinators provide different output of polyploid plants in a hybrid progeny, i.e. a quality of male gametes in different forms is different. A percent of triploid seedlings in different combinations of crossings varies from 0 to 100%.

Title: Wind Pollination of Apple Flowers Under Insect Exclusion Nets Questions the Insect-Dependent Pollination Model of Modern Apple Plantations
Snippet: Flowers of domesticated apple (Malus × domestica Borkh.) are perfect and complete. Apple is regarded as a self-infertile member of the Rosaceae family whose outcrossing is facilitated by the gametophytic self-incompatibility (GSI) system requiring pollen donors to possess at least one different S allele than the pistil to facilitate fertilization [1]. Pollination is a necessary step in apple fruit development, except for seedless cultivars (e.g., Spencer Seedless', Wellington Bloomless', and Rae Ime') whose fruit originate parthenocarpically [2]. In rare cases, self-compatible and cross-incompatible cultivars exist, albeit they are few [3]; the latter is limited to genetically similar varieties such as Cortland, Macoun, and McIntosh, and sports of a cultivar [4]. Self-pollination studies have demonstrated varying levels of self-fertility, ranging from ~2% in 'Fuji' and 'Golden Delicious' to 8% and 12% for 'Elstar' and 'Idared', respectively [5]. 

Pollination of most tree fruit species, including apple, is considered insect-dependent (Entomophilous), purportedly due to the relative mass of tree fruit pollen [6], in contrast Plants 2025, 14, 1196 2 of 14 with anemophilous species such as nut trees that depend on wind for pollen dispersal. The primary apple pollinators comprise species of bees and hoverflies [4,7]; the former are highly effective pollinators of apple flowers [8] and, thus, are typically introduced to apple plantations as managed hives of European honeybees (Apis mellifera) to ensure adequate fruit set for commercial yield [4]. An important agronomic consequence of current apple pollination practices is the 'oversetting' of fruit, necessitating the additional expense and often unpredictable practice of chemical fruitlet thinning [9].

Title: Identification of pollinizers for apple ‘SCS426 Venice
Snippet: Although presenting hermaphrodite flowers, apples (Malus × domestica Borkh.) depend on cross-pollination for the fertilization of the flowers and consequent fruit set. This necessity is due to the gametophytic self-incompatibility mechanism presented in most species of the genus Malus and in several genera of the Rosaceae family (Fujii et al. 2016). Most apple cultivars do not produce fruit by self-pollination or by crosses between genotypes that have the same alleles in the S-locus, responsible for gametophytic self-incompatibility control (Ramírez and Davenport 2013;Kasajima 2017). 

For this reason, most commercial apple orchards are composed of fruit-producing cultivars (scion cultivars) and at least another genotype used as a pollinizer. Pollinizers must coincide at flowering time with the scion cultivar (Matsumoto 2014;Albuquerque Junior et al. 2011). In addition, scion cultivars and pollinizers need to be genetically compatible (Orcheski and Brown 2012), since the pollen tube does not grow when the S-allele in the haploid cell of the pollen grain is the same to one of the two S-alleles expressed in the pistil (Matsumoto et al. 1999;Sassa et al. 2007). 

The gametophytic self-incompatibility is a barrier to identify and use compatible plants for directed crosses or pollination in the field that enables fruit set (de Nettancourt 1977). Likewise, fruit growers cannot produce fruit optimally when incompatible genotypes are grown in the orchards (Orcheski and Brown 2012). In order to ensure the formation of symmetrical fruit with normal shape development, at least one seed must be formed in four of the five fruit carpels (Denardi and Stuker 2008;Sheffield 2014). The normal apple shape formation is induced through hormones released by the developing embryos, so the ovule fertilization and the consequent seed formation in the carpels are necessary to obtain fruit with appropriate shape (Matsumoto et al. 2012).

Although presenting hermaphrodite flowers, apples (Malus × domestica Borkh.) depend on cross-pollination for the fertilization of the flowers and consequent fruit set. This necessity is due to the gametophytic self-incompatibility mechanism presented in most species of the genus Malus and in several genera of the Rosaceae family (Fujii et al. 2016). Most apple cultivars do not produce fruit by self-pollination or by crosses between genotypes that have the same alleles in the S-locus, responsible for gametophytic self-incompatibility control (Ramírez and Davenport 2013;Kasajima 2017). 

For this reason, most commercial apple orchards are composed of fruit-producing cultivars (scion cultivars) and at least another genotype used as a pollinizer. Pollinizers must coincide at flowering time with the scion cultivar (Matsumoto 2014;Albuquerque Junior et al. 2011). In addition, scion cultivars and pollinizers need to be genetically compatible (Orcheski and Brown 2012), since the pollen tube does not grow when the S-allele in the haploid cell of the pollen grain is the same to one of the two S-alleles expressed in the pistil (Matsumoto et al. 1999;Sassa et al. 2007). 

The gametophytic self-incompatibility is a barrier to identify and use compatible plants for directed crosses or pollination in the field that enables fruit set (de Nettancourt 1977). Likewise, fruit growers cannot produce fruit optimally when incompatible genotypes are grown in the orchards (Orcheski and Brown 2012). In order to ensure the formation of symmetrical fruit with normal shape development, at least one seed must be formed in four of the five fruit carpels (Denardi and Stuker 2008;Sheffield 2014). The normal apple shape formation is induced through hormones released by the developing embryos, so the ovule fertilization and the consequent seed formation in the carpels are necessary to obtain fruit with appropriate shape (Matsumoto et al. 2012).

Triploid apples, generally characterized by their large fruits, have been very attractive to both growers and consumers: old cultivars such as 'Gravenstein', 'Baldwin', 'Rhode Island Greening', 'Blenheim Orange', 'Stayman Winesap', 'Tompkins County King', as well as newer cultivars 'Jonagold' and 'Mutsu' [28]. The fertility of triploids has, however, been found to be lower than that of the diploids and tetraploids, but rarely zero and often with differences between cultivars [1], [9], [28]. This character appeals to both apple breeders and growers because of less labour needed for blossom and fruit thinning in triploids [28]. Despite years of effort, attempts of chromosome doubling using colchicine [36] and endosperm culture [28] have not contributed to release of triploid apple cultivars. More than 90% commercially superior triploid apple cultivars have proved to be produced by sexual polyploidization [28]. Thus, diploid crosses remain the principal method to breed apple triploid cultivars. 

There are approximately 8,000 diploid apple cultivars in the world, but fewer than 50 are triploids [28]. Given importance of triploid cultivars in the apple industry, we present a protocol using co-dominant markers aimed to efficiently identify a small number of triploid seedlings in a large population and thus to accelerate the triploid breeding program (Figure S1). In addition, parental genetic backgrounds influenced the frequency of triploids in the diploid F 1 seedlings (Table 1), thus parents should be carefully chosen for successful triploid breeding.

documents.title: Comparing diploid and triploid apples from a diverse collection
documents.snippet: Apples (Malus X. domestica Borkh.) are an economically important fruit species and the focus of continuing breeding efforts around the world. While most apple varieties are diploid, ploidy levels vary across the species, and triploids may be used in breeding despite poor fertility. The impact of ploidy on agricultural traits in apple is not well understood but is an important factor to consider when breeding new apple varieties. Here, we use mean heterozygosity values to categorize 970 apple accessions as diploid or triploid and then contrast apples of varying ploidy levels across 10 agriculturally important traits with sample sizes ranging from 427 to 928 accessions. After correction for multiple testing, we determine that triploids have significantly higher phenolic content. By examining historical release dates for apple varieties, our findings suggest that contemporary breeding programs are primarily releasing diploid varieties, and triploids tend to be older varieties. Ultimately, our results suggest that phenotypic differences between diploids and triploids are subtle and often insignificant indicating that triploids may not provide substantial benefit above diploids to apple breeding programs.

Below is a concise, evidence-based guide to what determines whether triploid apple genetic material remains viable when used as a parent in breeding programs.

Summary
- Triploid apples are commonly used for traits like large fruit size and vigorous growth, but their fertility is generally reduced relative to diploids and tetraploids and varies markedly by cultivar, which constrains their effectiveness as parents. <cite id="9262b49c-0">Triploid apples have lower fertility than diploids and tetraploids, though not zero, and cultivar differences are substantial</cite> <cite id="9262b49c-2">Uneven ploidy causes fewer balanced gametes and reduced fertility, making triploids challenging to use as effective parents; historically, many triploid parents were dubbed “breeding dead ends” because they rarely produced offspring</cite>. 
- Viability of triploid parents hinges on meiotic regularity, pollen quality, S-allele compatibility, choice of the other parent (ploidy and genome background), and maternal/post‑zygotic processes (seed/fruit set, endosperm behavior, embryo rescue). <cite id="1c2c2b0f-0">Triploid cultivars often show reduced pollen viability and germination due to asymmetry in meiosis, with Jonagold (a triploid) exhibiting notably low values</cite> <cite id="9262b49c-4">When a triploid is the maternal parent, female meiosis is highly irregular, producing variable gamete chromosome complements (n=17, 34, or 51), so zygote ploidy depends on the partner gamete; polyploid progeny may arise only via specific combinations, including fusion of unreduced female gametes with haploid pollen</cite> <cite id="1ed6a3ea-0">Interspecific crosses can suffer low fertilization and post‑zygotic barriers such as endosperm abortion, often necessitating embryo rescue; wild Malus sieversii is highly sexually compatible with M. domestica and diversifies S‑alleles to reduce incompatibility</cite>.

Mechanistic determinants: meiosis and gamete formation
- Reduced fertility in triploids originates from irregular first-division meiosis in pollen sacs (microsporogenesis), leading to high degeneracy of pollen and variable gamete chromosome numbers. <cite id="1c2c2b0f-0">In triploids, mature anthers often contain ~90% degenerated pollen attributed to asymmetry in meiosis, with triploid cultivars like Jonagold showing low viability and germination</cite>. 
- In triploid seed parents, meiosis can produce euploid or unreduced gametes (e.g., n=34), yielding unpredictable zygote ploidies upon fertilization with diploid-like pollen (n=17). <cite id="9262b49c-4">Non-diploid-like meiosis in a triploid parent leads to highly variable female gametes (n=17, 34, 51), enabling diploid, triploid, or tetraploid offspring depending on the male gamete; polyploid recovery via triploid parents is rare unless specific unreduced gametes fuse</cite>. 
- Seed/fruit set requires fertilization of multiple ovules and formation of at least one functional embryo to trigger carpel hormonal signals; triploid maternal genotypes with poor fertilization success will produce low fruit set. <cite id="1ed6a3ea-4">Most apple cultivars are hermaphrodite but depend on cross‑pollination because of gametophytic self‑incompatibility; at least one seed must develop in four of five carpels for normal fruit shape, as embryos drive hormonal cues for fruit development</cite>.

Parental ploidy and crossing design
- Pollen parent ploidy and fertility strongly determine triploid frequency in progeny: diploid pollen often yields diploid progeny; diploid × tetraploid crosses are the standard route to triploids. <cite id="9262b49c-0">Diploid × diploid crosses can yield triploid seedlings via sexual polyploidization; chromosome doubling has rarely been used to release triploids, so diploid crosses remain the principal method</cite> <cite id="9262b49c-3">Crossing diploids with tetraploids generally produces triploid progeny; triploid cultivars often have higher valued traits, though benefits are cultivar- and goal-dependent</cite>. 
- Tetraploid male parents can be efficient donors of diploid gametes and produce high-quality triploid crosses. <cite id="1c2c2b0f-1">Tetraploid apple forms selected as donors of diploid gametes provide sufficient fertile pollen and carry disease resistance (e.g., scab Vf/Vm), supporting adaptive triploid cultivar development</cite> <cite id="1c2c2b0f-2">A tetraploid (4x) with irregular but largely correct meiosis produced 77.7% correct tetrads and, when used as pollinator, yielded 80% triploid progeny in a test cross; abnormal meiotic pictures did not preclude high viable pollen</cite> <cite id="1c2c2b0f-3">In diploid × tetraploid crosses, triploid frequency varies from 0 to 100% depending on pollinator quality; tetraploid as pollinator can efficiently supply diploid male gametes</cite>. 
- Cultivar-specific outcomes illustrate that not all triploids are equal: Jonagold (a triploid) produced mostly diploid progeny from a triploid seed parent with very low polyploid recovery, whereas other triploid crosses can recover polyploids via unreduced gametes. <cite id="9262b49c-4">From a triploid ‘Jonagold’ seed parent, only 1.9% of progeny were polyploid (triploid/tetraploid) while 32.6% were diploid, indicating that polyploid recovery depends on specific gamete combinations (e.g., n=34 female × n=17 male)</cite>. 
- Choice of diploid seed parents can influence triploid frequency; parental genetic backgrounds affect the fraction of triploids among F1s. <cite id="9262b49c-0">Parental genetic backgrounds influence the frequency of triploids in F1 seedlings, so parents must be carefully chosen to enrich for triploids</cite>.

Maternal and seed-parenthood genome background
- Seed parent genome (domestica vs sieversii) affects compatibility, fertilization efficiency, and post‑zygotic viability, often necessitating embryo rescue in interspecific transfers. <cite id="1ed6a3ea-0">Crossing into or out of M. sieversii can face low fertilization efficiency and endosperm abortion, requiring embryo rescue; M. sieversii is highly sexually compatible with M. domestica and supplies diverse S‑alleles to mitigate incompatibility</cite> <cite id="1ed6a3ea-2">Embryo rescue can transfer desirable genes across Malus species but often shows low plantlet production due to post‑zygotic abortion; auxin/cytokinin/gibberellin supplementation improves germination of rescued embryos</cite>.

- Triploid seed parents may also benefit from alternative nuclear backgrounds (e.g., tetraploid donors) that supply diploid gametes and improve zygote viability. <cite id="1c2c2b0f-2">Using tetraploid pollinizers selected for diploid gamete donation produced a high proportion of triploid progeny and high pollen viability, supporting robust crosses</cite>.

Title: Analysis on Unveiling the Natural Dynamics of Parthenocarpy and Self-Compatibility in Apple Trees
Snippet: Apple (Malus domestica) is self-incompatible and typically requires cross-pollination for seed and fruit development. Parthenocarpy (fruit development without fertilization) and self-compatibility (fruit set without external pollen) are highly desirable traits in apple breeding, as they ensure consistent fruit production and quality without cross-pollination. Flowers were bagged before opening to prevent cross-pollination. If fruit developed from the bagged flowers, it indicated the presence of self-compatibility or parthenocarpy, depending on whether the fruit contained seeds. We observed and scored a range of phenotypic expressions among accessions, from weak to strong in both parthenocarpy and potential self-compatibility. Strong parthenocarpy was observed in 5.95% of wild Malus species accessions and 3.44% of M. domestica accessions. Snippet: Although presenting hermaphrodite flowers, apples (Malus × domestica Borkh.) depend on cross-pollination for the fertilization of the flowers and consequent fruit set. This necessity is due to the gametophytic self-incompatibility mechanism presented in most species of the genus Malus and in several genera of the Rosaceae family (Fujii et al. 2016). Most apple cultivars do not produce fruit by self-pollination or by crosses between genotypes that have the same alleles in the S-locus, responsible for gametophytic self-incompatibility control (Ramírez and Davenport 2013;Kasajima 2017). 

For this reason, most commercial apple orchards are composed of fruit-producing cultivars (scion cultivars) and at least another genotype used as a pollinizer. Pollinizers must coincide at flowering time with the scion cultivar (Matsumoto 2014;Albuquerque Junior et al. 2011). In addition, scion cultivars and pollinizers need to be genetically compatible (Orcheski and Brown 2012), since the pollen tube does not grow when the S-allele in the haploid cell of the pollen grain is the same to one of the two S-alleles expressed in the pistil (Matsumoto et al. 1999;Sassa et al. 2007).

In order to ensure the formation of symmetrical fruit with normal shape development, at least one seed must be formed in four of the five fruit carpels (Denardi and Stuker 2008;Sheffield 2014). Below is a concise, evidence-based guide to what determines whether triploid apple genetic material remains viable when used as a parent in breeding programs.

Summary
- Triploid apples are commonly used for traits like large fruit size and vigorous growth, but their fertility is generally reduced relative to diploids and tetraploids and varies markedly by cultivar, which constrains their effectiveness as parents. <cite id="9262b49c-0">Triploid apples have lower fertility than diploids and tetraploids, though not zero, and cultivar differences are substantial</cite> <cite id="9262b49c-2">Uneven ploidy causes fewer balanced gametes and reduced fertility, making triploids challenging to use as effective parents; historically, many triploid parents were dubbed “breeding dead ends” because they rarely produced offspring</cite>. 
- Viability of triploid parents hinges on meiotic regularity, pollen quality, S-allele compatibility, choice of the other parent (ploidy and genome background), and maternal/post‑zygotic processes (seed/fruit set, endosperm behavior, embryo rescue). <cite id="1c2c2b0f-0">Triploid cultivars often show reduced pollen viability and germination due to asymmetry in meiosis, with Jonagold (a triploid) exhibiting notably low values</cite> <cite id="9262b49c-4">When a triploid is the maternal parent, female meiosis is highly irregular, producing variable gamete chromosome complements (n=17, 34, or 51), so zygote ploidy depends on the partner gamete; polyploid progeny may arise only via specific combinations, including fusion of unreduced female gametes with haploid pollen</cite> <cite id="1ed6a3ea-0">Interspecific crosses can suffer low fertilization and post‑zygotic barriers such as endosperm abortion, often necessitating embryo rescue; wild Malus sieversii is highly sexually compatible with M. domestica and diversifies S‑alleles to reduce incompatibility</cite>.

Mechanistic determinants: meiosis and gamete formation
- Reduced fertility in triploids originates from irregular first-division meiosis in pollen sacs (microsporogenesis), leading to high degeneracy of pollen and variable gamete chromosome numbers. <cite id="1c2c2b0f-0">In triploids, mature anthers often contain ~90% degenerated pollen attributed to asymmetry in meiosis, with triploid cultivars like Jonagold showing low viability and germination</cite>. 
- In triploid seed parents, meiosis can produce euploid or unreduced gametes (e.g., n=34), yielding unpredictable zygote ploidies upon fertilization with diploid-like pollen (n=17). <cite id="9262b49c-4">Non-diploid-like meiosis in a triploid parent leads to highly variable female gametes (n=17, 34, 51), enabling diploid, triploid, or tetraploid offspring depending on the male gamete; polyploid recovery via triploid parents is rare unless specific unreduced gametes fuse</cite>. 
- Seed/fruit set requires fertilization of multiple ovules and formation of at least one functional embryo to trigger carpel hormonal signals; triploid maternal genotypes with poor fertilization success will produce low fruit set. <cite id="1ed6a3ea-4">Most apple cultivars are hermaphrodite but depend on cross‑pollination because of gametophytic self‑incompatibility; at least one seed must develop in four of five carpels for normal fruit shape, as embryos drive hormonal cues for fruit development</cite>.

Parental ploidy and crossing design
- Pollen parent ploidy and fertility strongly determine triploid frequency in progeny: diploid pollen often yields diploid progeny; diploid × tetraploid crosses are the standard route to triploids. <cite id="9262b49c-0">Diploid × diploid crosses can yield triploid seedlings via sexual polyploidization; chromosome doubling has rarely been used to release triploids, so diploid crosses remain the principal method</cite> <cite id="9262b49c-3">Crossing diploids with tetraploids generally produces triploid progeny; triploid cultivars often have higher valued traits, though benefits are cultivar- and goal-dependent</cite>. 
- Tetraploid male parents can be efficient donors of diploid gametes and produce high-quality triploid crosses. <cite id="1c2c2b0f-1">Tetraploid apple forms selected as donors of diploid gametes provide sufficient fertile pollen and carry disease resistance (e.g., scab Vf/Vm), supporting adaptive triploid cultivar development</cite> <cite id="1c2c2b0f-2">A tetraploid (4x) with irregular but largely correct meiosis produced 77.7% correct tetrads and, when used as pollinator, yielded 80% triploid progeny in a test cross; abnormal meiotic pictures did not preclude high viable pollen</cite> <cite id="1c2c2b0f-3">In diploid × tetraploid crosses, triploid frequency varies from 0 to 100% depending on pollinator quality; tetraploid as pollinator can efficiently supply diploid male gametes</cite>. 
- Cultivar-specific outcomes illustrate that not all triploids are equal: Jonagold (a triploid) produced mostly diploid progeny from a triploid seed parent with very low polyploid recovery, whereas other triploid crosses can recover polyploids via unreduced gametes. <cite id="9262b49c-4">From a triploid ‘Jonagold’ seed parent, only 1.9% of progeny were polyploid (triploid/tetraploid) while 32.6% were diploid, indicating that polyploid recovery depends on specific gamete combinations (e.g., n=34 female × n=17 male)</cite>. 
- Choice of diploid seed parents can influence triploid frequency; parental genetic backgrounds affect the fraction of triploids among F1s. <cite id="9262b49c-0">Parental genetic backgrounds influence the frequency of triploids in F1 seedlings, so parents must be carefully chosen to enrich for triploids</cite>.

Maternal and seed-parenthood genome background
- Seed parent genome (domestica vs sieversii) affects compatibility, fertilization efficiency, and post‑zygotic viability, often necessitating embryo rescue in interspecific transfers. <cite id="1ed6a3ea-0">Crossing into or out of M. sieversii can face low fertilization efficiency and endosperm abortion, requiring embryo rescue; M. sieversii is highly sexually compatible with M. domestica and supplies diverse S‑alleles to mitigate incompatibility</cite> <cite id="1ed6a3ea-2">Embryo rescue can transfer desirable genes across Malus species but often shows low plantlet production due to post‑zygotic abortion; auxin/cytokinin/gibberellin supplementation improves germination of rescued embryos</cite>.

- Triploid seed parents may also benefit from alternative nuclear backgrounds (e.g., tetraploid donors) that supply diploid gametes and improve zygote viability. <cite id="1c2c2b0f-2">Using tetraploid pollinizers selected for diploid gamete donation produced a high proportion of triploid progeny and high pollen viability, supporting robust crosses</cite>.

Compatibility and pollination biology
- Gametophytic self‑incompatibility (S‑locus) and S‑allele identity determine whether pollen germinates and fertilizes within the same genotype or a compatible genotype; incompatibility is a major barrier when using triploids as parents. <cite id="1ed6a3ea-4">Apple is gametophytically self‑incompatible; pollination fails when pollen S‑allele matches either of the two S‑alleles expressed in the pistil, so scion and pollinizer must be genetically compatible and flower synchronously</cite>. 
- Triploid cultivars can be hermaphrodite but still require cross‑pollination; pollen quality and parental S‑compatibility govern fertilization success. <cite id="1ed6a3ea-4">Despite hermaphrodite flowers, apples depend on cross‑pollination; pollen tube growth and fruit set depend on S‑allele compatibility between pollen and pistil</cite>.

- Triploid parents may also be used as seed parents to produce diploid progeny (e.g., by supplying 2n eggs to diploid pollen), but outcomes vary and can be low unless maternal genotype and timing favor fertilization. <cite id="9262b49c-4">Triploid progeny can arise from specific euploid or unreduced gamete fusions; the distribution of gametes in triploids is highly variable, so diploid outcomes dominate unless 2n gametes fuse</cite>.

Practical determinants for breeding success with triploid parents
- Parent selection: choose triploid cultivars with documented fertility or histories of producing viable seed; favor triploids derived from diploid parents with robust meiosis, and consider tetraploid donors to supply diploid gametes. <cite id="9262b49c-0">Triploid frequency in F1s depends on parental backgrounds; careful parent selection increases the chance of recovering triploids</cite> <cite id="1c2c2b0f-1">Tetraploid forms with high pollen fertility and disease resistance are valuable as diploid gamete donors</cite> <cite id="9262b49c-4">Specific triploid cultivars like Jonagold can produce mostly diploid progeny with very low polyploid recovery, underscoring cultivar-specific viability</cite>. 
- S‑allele compatibility and pollination design: ensure reciprocal S‑allele differences between pollen and pistil; provide multiple compatible pollinizers and adjust orchard spacing/timing for synchrony. <cite id="1ed6a3ea-4">Pollinizers must coincide with scion at flowering and differ at the S‑locus; otherwise pollen tubes fail to grow and fruit set is reduced</cite>. 
- Pollen quality and load: screen pollen for viability/germination and use high-quality pollen sources (prefer tetraploid donors when possible); maintain adequate pollen load to achieve fertilization across ovules. <cite id="1c2c2b0f-0">Triploid cultivars often have low pollen viability and germination, reducing fertilization potential; Jonagold shows particularly low values</cite> <cite id="1c2c2b0f-2">Tetraploid pollinizers selected for diploid gamete donation showed high viable pollen and high triploid recovery in test crosses</cite>. 
- Maternal/maternal-genome effects: use seed parents with good seed set capacity and low endosperm rejection; consider M. sieversii seed parents or embryo rescue for interspecific crosses to overcome post‑zygotic barriers. <cite id="1ed6a3ea-0">M. sieversii improves compatibility and supplies diverse S‑alleles; interspecific crosses often require embryo rescue due to endosperm abortion</cite> <cite id="1ed6a3ea-2">Embryo rescue can transfer genes but typically yields limited plantlets due to reduced embryo viability</cite>. 
- Phenology and orchard design: ensure scion–pollinizer synchrony and adequate cross‑pollination to achieve fertilization of multiple ovules per flower, which is necessary for normal fruit set and viable seeds. <cite id="1ed6a3ea-4">Fruit set depends on cross‑pollination and at least one fertilized seed per carpel to trigger proper hormonal cues for fruit development</cite>. 
- Expect variability and set realistic targets: triploid parents can yield highly variable progeny ploidy; successful triploid breeding commonly relies on diploid × tetraploid crosses and careful selection from F1s, with polyploid recovery rates sometimes low to moderate depending on gamete ploidy. <cite id="9262b49c-0">Diploid crosses remain the principal route to triploid cultivars; chromosome doubling has not routinely produced released triploids</cite> <cite id="1c2c2b0f-3">Triploid recovery in diploid × tetraploid crosses can range from 0 to 100% depending on pollinator quality and gamete ploidy</cite>.

Cultivar and trait-specific notes
- Triploid breeding has historically struggled, but targeted crosses and marker-assisted selection can enrich for triploid seedlings. <cite id="9262b49c-0">Attempts to release triploid cultivars via colchicine or endosperm culture have been limited; most commercially successful triploids arose via sexual polyploidization from diploid parents; SNP markers can efficiently identify rare triploid seedlings, and parental choice affects triploid frequency</cite>. 
- Phenotypic benefits of triploids (larger fruit, vigor, disease resistance) may be cultivar- and goal‑dependent; breeding programs must weigh viability as parents against agronomic gains. <cite id="9262b49c-1">Across 970 accessions, phenotypic differences between diploids and triploids are subtle and often insignificant, implying triploids may not provide clear agronomic advantages over diploids</cite> <cite id="9262b49c-3">Triploids may show higher phenolic content and other small differences; commercial programs have largely favored diploids, with triploid commercial releases decreasing since 1900</cite>.

Key takeaways for viability of triploid apple genetic material as parents
- If used as seed parent: success depends on regular meiosis producing functional gametes, high pollen compatibility, and maternal capacity to set seed; tetraploid donors can stabilize diploid gamete supply and increase triploid recovery, while interspecific seed parents may require embryo rescue. <cite id="1c2c2b0f-0">Triploid pistils often produce mostly degenerate pollen and reduced fruit set due to gamete irregularity</cite> <cite id="9262b49c-4">Unpredictable gamete complements in triploids lead to variable zygote ploidy; polyploid recovery is rare unless specific unreduced gametes fuse</cite> <cite id="1ed6a3ea-0">M. sieversii seed parents improve compatibility and help overcome incompatibility and endosperm abortion with rescue</cite>.

- Quantitative outcomes vary widely by cultivar and cross; polyploid recovery from triploid parents can be extremely low or, under favorable unreduced gamete pairing, high. <cite id="9262b49c-4">In one triploid seed parent, polyploid progeny were 1.9% vs 32.6% diploids, illustrating narrow windows for polyploid recovery</cite>. 
- Mechanistic genotype-by-genotype interactions (e.g., Malus domestica × Malus sieversii vs within M. domestica) and timing effects require cultivar-specific protocols; broader cytogenetic mapping of meiosis in triploid apple accessions would clarify breeding guidelines. <cite id="9262b49c-2">Triploids are often “breeding dead ends” due to reduced fertility, but diploid parents can still produce occasional viable offspring, making their use context-dependent</cite> <cite id="1ed6a3ea-0">Interspecific crossings often require rescue due to endosperm abortion; diversifying S‑alleles and compatibility improves efficiency</cite>.
